questions.q: What does the Bronze layer hold in this pipeline's plan?
options: The raw daily extract exactly as it arrives, with no cleaning, casting, or deduplication
One row per calendar day, fully aggregated
Only rows that passed every validation check
A copy of the Gold table for backup purposes
questions.explain: Bronze is deliberately untouched — any cleaning happens downstream in Silver, so nothing is lost before you decide how to clean it.

questions.q: Why does Silver unify in-store and online records into the same shape, rather than keeping two separate tables?
options: Because Silver is the first place in the pipeline where the two channels stop being different things and become just "sales"
Because PySpark cannot read two different file formats in the same notebook
Because Bronze already unified them, so Silver just copies Bronze unchanged
Because Gold requires exactly two source tables as input
questions.explain: Schema unification happens in Silver on purpose — Bronze intentionally keeps the source-specific messiness, and Gold only needs one clean shape to aggregate.

questions.q: What is the grain of the gold.daily_sales_summary table, according to the plan?
options: One row per calendar day
One row per sale line item
One row per store per product
One row per original source file
questions.explain: Gold is the aggregated answer to Lesson 1's requirement — exactly one row per day, holding that day's total sales and order count.

questions.q: What is the one real capability a Delta table gives you that a plain folder of Parquet or CSV files doesn't?
options: A transaction log, enabling schema enforcement, time travel, and incremental updates via MERGE
Automatic translation of column names between English and other languages
Built-in Power BI report templates
A guarantee that the data is always sorted by date
questions.explain: The transaction log is what separates a Delta table from plain files — it's what later projects rely on to MERGE new data in rather than rebuilding from scratch.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist on writing the three-layer plan in plain English before opening a notebook?
options: Skipping the plan risks discovering required columns are undefined partway through writing the Silver transformation, forcing a rewrite
PySpark requires a written plan file to execute without errors
Plain English plans are a formal requirement of Delta Lake's transaction log
Because Bronze cannot be created without first creating Gold
questions.explain: The plan exists to avoid discovering mid-build that you didn't define what a required field is — a cheap problem to fix on paper, an expensive one to fix in code.
